books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, B. Cotton, Slavery, and the Southern Exception

primary_sources: The Old Plantation, attributed to John Rose, c. 1785-1790

stimulus.text: The Old Plantation, a watercolor painted in South Carolina around 1785-1790 and attributed to John Rose, shows enslaved people dancing to banjo music outside their quarters, with the planter's house and other cabins in the background.
stimulus.source_note: Painting viewed before writing: The Old Plantation, attributed to John Rose, c. 1785-1790, shared pool file u3/old-plantation-john-rose-1790.jpg, public domain. Painted before 1800; used here for the continuity of enslaved culture into the early republic, with its date stated.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, The Old Plantation, attributed to John Rose, c. 1785-1790, public domain
stem: The painting shows enslaved people dancing while one man plays a banjo. What does that scene most directly show about enslaved people's lives?

options.text: Enslaved people had no culture of their own
options.misconception: The painting shows music and dance, which are culture kept alive under slavery.

options.text: Enslaved people kept music and community life alive despite slavery
Enslaved people were free to leave the plantation at will
options.misconception: Enslaved people could not leave at will; the painting shows leisure time, not freedom.

options.text: Planters banned all music and dancing on plantations
options.misconception: The painting itself shows music and dancing happening on a plantation.

rationales.A: The painting shows music and dance, which are culture kept alive under slavery.
rationales.B: The banjo music and the dancing circle show enslaved people making music and community together in the time slavery allowed them.
rationales.C: Enslaved people could not leave at will. The painting shows leisure time, not freedom.
rationales.D: The painting itself shows music and dancing happening on a plantation.
rationales.general:
1. Read the image. A man plays the banjo while others dance in a circle outside their quarters.
2. Ask what that takes. Music and dance need a shared life, not just work side by side.
3. Name what it shows. Even under slavery, enslaved people kept a community life of their own.
Background: The banjo came from Africa, and its music carried African ways into Southern life.
Remember: leisure scenes can show a community that work scenes hide.
